detail:
The Ehlers-Danlos Society describes craniocervical instability (CCI) as a type of loose ligament condition in the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) that results in injury to the nervous system. CCI occurs when ligaments from the skull to the spine don't restrict unsafe movement. The Society notes that nervous damage from loose ligaments may explain slow development of movement skills, poor coordination, learning difficulties, headaches, and clumsiness in the EDS population, and that there is increased recognition of mechanisms of nerve injury from stretching and bending.

The Society places CCI among the neurological and spinal manifestations of EDS, in which overly moveable vertebrae can also lead to damage to discs, vertebrae, and nerves, and to worsening symptoms related to damage to the spinal cord. It states plainly that there are no established guidelines for treatment of CCI in EDS, though there is information available for the diagnosis and treatment of CCI in various other connective tissue disorders.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about craniocervical instability symptoms and evaluation.
summary: The Ehlers-Danlos Society describes craniocervical instability (CCI) as a loose ligament condition in the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes in which ligaments from the skull to the spine do not restrict unsafe movement, which can injure the nervous system.
takeaways: cci is a loose ligament condition at the skull and spine junction in eds
nerve injury from unsafe movement may explain headaches and poor coordination
there are no established treatment guidelines for cci in eds
title: Craniocervical instability: loose ligaments where the skull meets the spine
